entry.summary: I wrote this series as a running study log covering core Java mechanics, Spring Boot runtime behavior, and JPA/Hibernate internals. Writing them down in my own words helps bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and production intuition—making sure I can articulate the trade-offs clearly when it counts in technical rounds.
entry.content:
I wrote this series as a running study log covering core Java mechanics, Spring Boot runtime behavior, and JPA/Hibernate internals. Writing them down in my own words helps bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and production intuition—making sure I can articulate the trade-offs clearly when it counts in technical rounds.

Core Java​

1. ArrayList vs LinkedList — Internal Working​

  • ArrayList (Dynamic Array):
    • Memory: Elements sit side-by-side in one contiguous memory block.
    • Read O(1)O(1)O(1): Instant access by index using simple pointer math (base_address + index * size).
    • Insert/Delete O(n)O(n)O(n): Adding or removing anywhere except the tail forces all subsequent elements to shift in memory.
  • LinkedList (Doubly Linked List):
    • Memory: Independent node objects scattered across the heap, wired together via prev and next pointers.
    • Insert/Delete O(1)O(1)O(1): Re-linking pointers takes constant time once you already hold the target node reference.
    • Read O(n)O(n)O(n): Must walk node-by-node from the head or tail to reach an index.
  • The Production Reality:
    • In textbook theory, LinkedList wins for write-heavy cases.
    • In modern architectures, ArrayList almost always wins due to CPU cache locality (reading contiguous memory is orders of magnitude faster than chasing pointer references across random heap locations). Use ArrayList by default unless you have an explicit queue/deque need.

2. How HashMap Handles Collisions & Treeification​

Think of a HashMap like a row of numbered lockers (called buckets).

When you store a key-value pair, Java calculates a locker number using the key's hash code:

Locker Index=hash(key)(modcapacity)\text{Locker Index} = \text{hash}(\text{key}) \pmod{\text{capacity}}Locker Index=hash(key)(modcapacity)

A collision happens when two completely different keys calculate the exact same locker number.

What happens during a collision?​

  • Before Java 8:
    • The locker acted like a single line (a LinkedList).
    • New collisions were simply tacked onto the end.
    • If 10 items landed in the same locker, finding your key meant checking each item one-by-one from the front to the back.
    • Search speed in a crowded bucket: O(n)O(n)O(n) (linear time).
  • Java 8 and Newer (Treeification):
    • When a single bucket gets crowded (more than 8 items) and the total map capacity is at least 64, Java reorganizes that locker into a balanced Red-Black Tree.
    • Instead of scanning one-by-one, Java can divide and conquer using binary search.
    • Search speed inside the bucket improves from O(n)O(n)O(n) to O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn).
    • If items are removed and the bucket drops down to 6 items or fewer, Java turns it back into a simple list to save memory.

The Quick Takeaway​

SituationData Structure Inside BucketSearch Speed
Normal / Low CollisionsLinkedList (simple chain)O(1)O(1)O(1) on average, O(n)O(n)O(n) worst-case inside bucket
Crowded (> 8 items)Red-Black Tree (balanced branches)O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn)

Why this matters in real life: It prevents an app from freezing up if thousands of keys accidentally (or maliciously) crowd into the same locker.

3. Comparable vs Comparator​

When you want to sort a list of objects in Java, the JVM needs to know: "Which one comes first?"

Java gives you two interfaces to answer this question:

  • Comparable: The object decides how to sort itself (default order).
  • Comparator: An external helper decides how to sort two objects (custom order).

Quick Comparison Table​

FeatureComparableComparator
Packagejava.lang (no import needed)java.util (requires import)
MethodcompareTo(Object other)compare(Object o1, Object o2)
Philosophy"I know my natural order""Someone else decides how to sort us"
Modify Original Class?Yes (you must edit source code)No (can pass as external logic/lambda)
Sorting StrategiesExactly one natural orderMultiple (sort by name, sort by price, etc.)

1. Comparable: Internal / Natural Order​

Use Comparable when your class has an obvious, universal way to be sorted (like numbers in ascending order or people by ID).

// Modifies the class directly
public class Product implements Comparable<Product> {
    private int id;
    private String name;

    public Product(int id, String name) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Product other) {
        // Natural sort by ID ascending
        return Integer.compare(this.id, other.id);
    }
}

// Usage:
Collections.sort(productList); // Automatically uses compareTo()

2. Comparator: External / Flexible Order​

Use Comparator when you need alternative ways to sort, or when you cannot modify the original class (e.g., third-party library classes).

// No changes needed to the Product class!

// Option A: Sort by Name ascending (modern lambda style)
Comparator<Product> byName = (p1, p2) -> p1.getName().compareTo(p2.getName());

// Option B: Sort by Name using Comparator builder methods
Comparator<Product> byNameClean = Comparator.comparing(Product::getName);

// Usage:
productList.sort(byNameClean);

Mental Model to Remember​

  • If a class should have a single default identity order, implement Comparable (this.compareTo(that)).
  • If you want different views (e.g., sort by price low-to-high, high-to-low, or by date), write a Comparator (compare(a, b)).

4. Immutability in Java​

An immutable object is an object whose internal state cannot change once it has been constructed. Once created, it is completely read-only for its entire lifetime.

The 5 Rules to Build an Immutable Class​

To make a class truly immutable, lock down every way data can be modified:

  1. Make the class final: Prevents other classes from extending it and overriding methods to introduce mutable behavior.
  2. Make all fields private and final: private blocks direct external access, and final guarantees each field is assigned only once.
  3. Do not provide setters: Remove all setX() mutator methods.
  4. Initialize everything via the constructor: Assign all values during instantiation. If fields are mutable objects (like List or Date), make defensive copies inside the constructor.
  5. Return defensive copies in getters: Never return the direct reference to an internal mutable field. Return a clone or an unmodifiable copy so callers cannot modify your internal state from the outside.

Code Example: Before & After​

// ❌ MUTABLE: Dangerous because callers can modify the internal list
public class MutableUser {
    private String name;
    private List<String> roles;

    public MutableUser(String name, List<String> roles) {
        this.name = name;
        this.roles = roles; // Leaks external reference!
    }

    public List<String> getRoles() {
        return roles; // Callers can do: user.getRoles().add("ADMIN");
    }
}
// ✅ IMMUTABLE: Completely locked down and thread-safe
public final class ImmutableUser {
    private final String name;
    private final List<String> roles;

    public ImmutableUser(String name, List<String> roles) {
        this.name = name;
        // Defensive copy on constructor input
        this.roles = (roles != null) ? List.copyOf(roles) : List.of();
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public List<String> getRoles() {
        // Returns an unmodifiable list (or deep copy)
        return roles;
    }
}

Modern Java Shortcut: From Java 14 onwards, you can often use record (public record ImmutableUser(String name, List<String> roles) {}) to get immutability mechanics out of the box (just make sure mutable references like lists are wrapped defensively).

Why Do We Care? (The Big Win)​

  • Thread Safety for Free: Because state cannot change, multiple threads can read the object simultaneously without locks or synchronization issues.
  • Safe as Map Keys: Immutable objects (like String or Integer) never change their hash code after creation, preventing lost-key bugs in HashMap.
  • Predictable Architecture: Functions cannot produce unexpected side effects by secretly altering passed arguments.

5. ExecutorService & Thread Pools​

Creating a new thread in Java (new Thread()) is expensive: each thread allocates its own stack memory (typically ~1MB) and demands OS-level context switching.

Instead of creating threads by hand and destroying them after each task, a Thread Pool keeps a pool of reusable worker threads alive, while ExecutorService manages their lifecycle and schedules your tasks.

Why Use a Thread Pool?​

  • Eliminates Thread Creation Overhead: Reuses idle threads instead of allocating new OS threads from scratch.
  • Resource & Crash Control: Caps the maximum number of concurrent threads to prevent exhausting system memory and causing an OutOfMemoryError.
  • Separates Work from Execution: You submit tasks (Runnable / Callable), while the framework handles queueing, execution, and worker lifecycles.

4 Common Types of Thread Pools​

Java provides pre-configured thread pools via the Executors factory class:

Pool TypeHow It BehavesBest Use Case
FixedThreadPool(n)Has a fixed number of threads. Excess tasks wait in an unbounded queue.Predictable, CPU-bound workloads where you want strict resource limits.
CachedThreadPool()Dynamically grows thread count on demand. Tears down threads that idle past 60 seconds.Many short-lived, bursty asynchronous tasks.
SingleThreadExecutor()Exactly one worker thread processing tasks strictly one after another.Tasks that must run in guaranteed sequential order without race conditions.
ScheduledThreadPool(n)Executes tasks with an initial delay or repeatedly at a fixed rate.Background maintenance tasks, cache cleanups, and heartbeats.

Practical Code Pattern​

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class ThreadPoolExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Create a pool with 3 reusable threads
        ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3);

        // 2. Submit tasks to the pool
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
            final int taskId = i;
            executor.submit(() -> {
                System.out.println("Processing task " + taskId + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
            });
        }

        // 3. Graceful shutdown: stop accepting new tasks, finish pending ones
        executor.shutdown();
        try {
            if (!executor.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
                executor.shutdownNow(); // Force stop if tasks hang
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            executor.shutdownNow();
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
}

Production Reality Check​

Avoid raw Executors.newFixedThreadPool() or Executors.newCachedThreadPool() in high-throughput enterprise systems:

  • FixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue (LinkedBlockingQueue), which can grow infinitely and crash the application with an OutOfMemoryError if producers outpace consumers.
  • CachedThreadPool uses unbounded thread creation, which can spawn thousands of threads under load and exhaust OS thread limits.

Best Practice: Build your pool explicitly using new ThreadPoolExecutor(...) where you define a bounded queue, core and max pool sizes, and a clear rejection policy (like discarding or running on the caller's thread).

6. synchronized vs Lock API​

When multiple threads try to update the same shared resource at the same time, you risk data corruption (race conditions). Java gives you two ways to lock the door so only one thread enters at a time:

  • synchronized: Built directly into the Java language and JVM.
  • Lock API (java.util.concurrent.locks): A flexible, code-level toolset introduced in Java 5.

Feature Comparison​

FeaturesynchronizedLock API (ReentrantLock)
LevelJVM-level keywordJava API-level class
FlexibilityLow (block-scoped or method-scoped)High (can lock in one method and unlock in another)
Try Lock (Non-blocking)No (thread blocks indefinitely until lock is free)Yes (tryLock() attempts to acquire without waiting)
TimeoutsNo (will wait forever)Yes (tryLock(timeout, timeUnit))
InterruptibleNo (cannot abort a thread waiting for the lock)Yes (lockInterruptibly())
Fairness PolicyNo (cannot guarantee first-come, first-served)Yes (supports fair lock ordering)
Unlock MechanismAutomatic (released when block exits, even on exceptions)Manual (must be placed inside a finally block)

1. synchronized: Clean & Automatic​

Best for simple use cases where you just want to guard a critical block without extra configuration.

public class Counter {
    private int count = 0;

    // Automatic acquire on entry, automatic release on exit
    public synchronized void increment() {
        count++;
    }
}

2. Lock API (ReentrantLock): Advanced Control​

Best when you need to avoid deadlocks with timeouts or bail out if a lock is currently unavailable.

import java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class InventoryService {
    private final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    public void updateStock() {
        // ALWAYS use try-finally so locks are never left abandoned!
        lock.lock();
        try {
            // Critical section
            System.out.println("Stock updated safely");
        } finally {
            lock.unlock(); // Guaranteed release even if an exception occurs
        }
    }

    public boolean tryUpdateStockWithTimeout() throws InterruptedException {
        // Tries to get the lock for up to 2 seconds, moves on if unavailable
        if (lock.tryLock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            try {
                // Critical section
                return true;
            } finally {
                lock.unlock();
            }
        }
        // Fallback logic if the lock was busy
        System.out.println("Could not acquire lock, proceeding with fallback");
        return false;
    }
}

Rule of Thumb​

  • Default to synchronized when standard mutual exclusion is all you need—it's simpler, less prone to developer error (no risk of forgettingunlock()), and heavily optimized by the JVM.
  • Reach for ReentrantLock when you specifically need non-blocking attempts (tryLock()), timeouts to prevent deadlocks, or thread interruption.

7. ConcurrentHashMap Thread-Safety​

Standard HashMap is not thread-safe: concurrent writes can lead to infinite loops or corrupted state. Collections.synchronizedMap() fixes this, but it locks the entire map on every single read or write, choking throughput.

ConcurrentHashMap solves this by offering high performance and thread safety simultaneously—allowing completely non-blocking concurrent reads alongside safe partial writes.

How Thread-Safety Evolved​

MechanismPre-Java 8 (Segment-Based)Java 8+ (Bucket-Level Fine Grained)
Locking UnitWhole Segment (array of sub-maps)Individual Bucket Head Node
Default ConcurrencyUp to 16 threads writing concurrently (default 16 segments)Scalable to the number of buckets
Internal ToolReentrantLock per segmentCAS + narrow synchronized blocks

Under the Hood: Java 8+ Mechanics​

  1. Lock-Free Reads (O(1)O(1)O(1)):
    • Reads (get()) never acquire a lock.
    • Internal table node values and next pointers are declared volatile, guaranteeing immediate visibility across thread caches without synchronization overhead.
  2. Empty Bucket Insertion via CAS:
    • When inserting into a bucket that is currently empty, it does not lock.
    • It uses low-level Compare-And-Swap (CAS): if no other thread slipped in during that CPU cycle, the node is inserted completely lock-free.
  3. Collided Bucket Insertion via synchronized:
    • If the bucket already has items (a collision), it locks only the first node of that specific bucket (synchronized (f)).
    • Threads targeting different buckets write simultaneously with zero contention.

Quick Code Example​

import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

public class CacheService {
    // Thread-safe map for high-concurrency read/write workloads
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> pageViews = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void recordView(String path) {
        // Atomic compute: thread-safe without manual locks
        pageViews.compute(path, (key, count) -> (count == null) ? 1 : count + 1);
    }

    public int getViewCount(String path) {
        // Fully non-blocking read
        return pageViews.getOrDefault(path, 0);
    }
}

Key Takeaway​

  • Use ConcurrentHashMap whenever multiple threads read and write to the same map concurrently.
  • Never use compound operations blindly: Calling if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) is two separate operations and creates a race condition. Always rely on atomic methods like putIfAbsent(), computeIfAbsent(), or merge().

8. The volatile Keyword​

In modern CPUs, each core maintains its own high-speed hardware cache (L1/L2/L3). When a thread reads a variable, it often copies it into its local CPU cache rather than fetching from main memory (RAM) every time.

The volatile keyword tells the JVM: "Never cache this variable in a CPU register. Always read from and write directly to main memory."

Core Characteristics​

  • Guarantees Visibility: Any update written by one thread is immediately visible to any other thread reading that field.
  • Does NOT Guarantee Atomicity: It prevents stale reads, but it does not protect compound operations (e.g., read-modify-write actions like count++) from race conditions.
  • Prevents Instruction Reordering: Establishes a happens-before memory barrier, ensuring the compiler or CPU does not rearrange read/write instructions around the volatile access.

Visibility vs. Atomicity: The Classic Trap​

// ❌ ATOMICITY TRAP: volatile is NOT enough here!
private volatile int counter = 0;

public void increment() {
    counter++;
    // Under the hood, counter++ is 3 distinct CPU steps:
    // 1. Read counter
    // 2. Increment by 1
    // 3. Write counter back
    // Two threads executing this concurrently will still overwrite each other!
}

// ✅ FIX FOR ATOMICITY:
// Use AtomicInteger (uses hardware CAS under the hood)
private final AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(0);

public void increment() {
    counter.incrementAndGet();
}

Best Use Case: State & Termination Flags​

Because volatile guarantees instant visibility without the locking overhead of synchronized, it is ideal for simple status flags and shutdown triggers.

public class BackgroundWorker implements Runnable {
    // Thread-safe termination flag
    private volatile boolean running = true; //[cite: 1]

    public void stopWorker() {
        this.running = false; // Writes straight to RAM[cite: 1]
    }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        while (running) { // Always reads current state from RAM[cite: 1]
            // Process queue items...
        }
        System.out.println("Worker shut down safely.");
    }
}

Quick Mental Model​

  • Need instant cross-thread visibility for a single read/write? →\rightarrow→ volatile
  • Need atomic compound operations (like counters or accumulators)? →\rightarrow→ AtomicInteger / AtomicReference
  • Need complex multi-variable synchronization? →\rightarrow→ synchronized or ReentrantLock

entry.title: Walkthrough: Web Visitor Counter Lambda
entry.summary: Inspired by Cloud Resume Challenge, I started building a high-performance, strongly typed AWS Lambda function backed by Amazon DynamoDB for atomic web visitor counting, triggered via Amazon API Gateway HTTP API (Payload v2).
entry.content:
Inspired by Cloud Resume Challenge, I started building a high-performance, strongly typed AWS Lambda function backed by Amazon DynamoDB for atomic web visitor counting, triggered via Amazon API Gateway HTTP API (Payload v2).

Currently I have finished working on the Lambda function, and I am working towards the deployment of the API Gateway HTTP API and DynamoDB table. This post is a walkthrough of the source code, testing, and build process, that I and AI pair-programmed together. The source code is available on GitHub.

What Was Built​

1. Source Architecture​

  • src/types.ts: Strongly typed models for CounterRecord, CounterResponse, ErrorResponse, and AppConfig.
  • src/config.ts: Environment variable loader for TABLE_NAME, ALLOW_ORIGIN, DEFAULT_PAGE_ID, and AWS_REGION.
  • src/utils.ts: CORS headers, API Gateway v2 response builders, and pageId sanitization (validates characters and restricts max length to 128 characters).
  • src/counter.ts: DynamoDB atomic operations using AWS SDK v3 DynamoDBDocumentClient:
    • incrementCounter: Uses atomic update expression: 
      SET #count = if_not_exists(#count, :zero) + :inc, #updatedAt = :now
    • getCounter: Reads count without incrementing; returns { count: 0, updatedAt: null } for unvisited pages.
  • src/handler.ts: Main AWS Lambda handler (APIGatewayProxyHandlerV2):
    • Handles OPTIONS CORS preflight requests (HTTP 204).
    • Routes POST to increment counter.
    • Routes GET to read counter.
    • Returns HTTP 405 for unsupported HTTP methods.
    • Returns HTTP 400 for malformed input or invalid pageId.
    • Returns HTTP 500 for missing config or database errors.

2. Testing & Tooling​

  • package.json: Configured with @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb, @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb, esbuild, jest, ts-jest, and aws-sdk-client-mock.
  • jest.config.js: Unit test configuration with ts-jest and coverage thresholds.
  • tests/counter.test.ts: Unit tests for DynamoDB atomic increments and reads.
  • tests/handler.test.ts: End-to-end event routing, CORS, query/body parsing, and error handling.
  • tests/config.test.ts: Environment variable validation tests.
  • tests/utils.test.ts: Sanitization, validation, and CORS tests.
  • README.md: Documentation including DynamoDB table creation, IAM permissions, API Gateway HTTP API setup, and frontend client snippet.

Validation Results​

1. TypeScript Strict Typecheck​

npm run typecheck

Passed with 0 errors.

2. Jest Test Suite with Coverage​

npm run test:coverage
PASS tests/config.test.ts
PASS tests/utils.test.ts
PASS tests/counter.test.ts
PASS tests/handler.test.ts

------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------
File        | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines | Uncovered Line #s
------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------
All files   |    96.8 |    90.69 |   85.71 |    96.8 |
 config.ts  |     100 |    88.88 |     100 |     100 |
 counter.ts |     100 |       80 |     100 |     100 |
 handler.ts |    93.1 |      100 |      50 |    93.1 |
 utils.ts   |   97.29 |    94.11 |     100 |   97.29 |
------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------

Test Suites: 4 passed, 4 total
Tests:       33 passed, 33 total

3. Build & Package Verification​

npm run package
  • Bundled via esbuild to CommonJS Node.js 20 target.
  • Produced dist/visitor-counter.zip (577 KB), verified dist/index.js exports handler.

entry.title: How to setup Husky and Lint-Staged
entry.summary: In modern software development, maintaining code quality and consistency across a team is crucial. When multiple developers work on a single codebase, differences in formatting, syntax styles, and simple errors can lead to messy pull requests and broken builds. This is where Git hooks, specifically pre-commit hooks, become incredibly valuable.
entry.content:
In modern software development, maintaining code quality and consistency across a team is crucial. When multiple developers work on a single codebase, differences in formatting, syntax styles, and simple errors can lead to messy pull requests and broken builds. This is where Git hooks, specifically pre-commit hooks, become incredibly valuable.

Two of the most powerful tools in the JavaScript ecosystem for managing Git hooks and code quality are Husky and Lint-Staged.

In this post, we'll explore what these tools are, why they are important, how to set them up, and how to test your configuration locally.

What are Husky and Lint-Staged?​

Husky​

Husky is a tool that allows you to easily tie scripts to Git hooks. Git hooks are scripts that Git executes before or after events such as: commit, push, and receive. Husky makes it simple to manage these hooks within your package.json or as separate script files, ensuring they are automatically installed for everyone who works on the project.

Lint-Staged​

Lint-Staged is a tool that allows you to run linters (like ESLint, Prettier, or cspell) against staged git files and don't let it slip into your codebase. Running linters on the entire project can be slow. Lint-Staged solves this by only running checks on files that are actively being modified and staged for a commit.

Why is it Important?​

  1. Catches Errors Early: By running linting, formatting, and spell checks on every commit, you catch simple mistakes before they even leave your local machine or trigger a CI build.
  2. Enforces Consistency: It ensures that all code pushed to the repository adheres to the team's defined standards (e.g., Prettier formatting, ESLint rules).
  3. Improves Code Reviews: When the code is consistently formatted, code reviews can focus on the actual logic and architecture rather than nitpicking spacing or syntax issues.
  4. Saves CI Time: Failing fast locally means your continuous integration (CI) pipeline doesn't have to waste time running jobs that fail on trivial style errors.

How to Set It Up​

Let's walk through setting up Husky and Lint-Staged to run ESLint, Prettier, and a spell checker (cspell) on pre-commit.

1. Install Dependencies​

First, ensure you have Husky, Lint-Staged, and your desired linters installed as devDependencies:

npm install --save-dev husky lint-staged eslint prettier cspell

2. Initialize Husky​

Run the Husky initialization script. This sets up the .husky directory and prepares Git to use it:

npx husky init

This command typically adds a prepare script in your package.json to ensure Husky is installed automatically after npm install.

{
  "scripts": {
    "prepare": "husky"
  }
}

3. Create a Pre-commit Hook​

Next, we need to instruct Husky to run lint-staged before every commit.

If npx husky init created a default pre-commit hook (usually echoing something or running npm test), you can overwrite it. Run the following command or edit the .husky/pre-commit file directly:

echo "npx lint-staged" > .husky/pre-commit

4. Configure Lint-Staged​

Finally, configure lint-staged in your package.json to define which tools run on which files. Here is an example configuration:

{
  "lint-staged": {
    "**/*.{md,mdx}": "cspell lint",
    "**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx,json,md,mdx,css}": "prettier --write",
    "src/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}": "eslint"
  }
}

Explanation of the config:

  • **/*.{md,mdx}: Runs the spell checker (cspell) on all Markdown and MDX files.
  • **/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx,json,md,mdx,css}: Runs Prettier to automatically format code. The --write flag tells Prettier to save the formatted changes back to the files.
  • src/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}: Runs ESLint on your source code to catch potential logic errors or rule violations.

How to Test It Locally​

Once configured, testing the setup is straightforward.

  1. Make a Change: Modify a file that matches your lint-staged configuration. For example, add some unformatted code to a JavaScript file or a typo to a Markdown file.
  2. Stage the File: 
    git add path/to/your/file.js
  3. Attempt a Commit: 
    git commit -m "Test husky setup"

What should happen?

  • Husky intercepts the commit process.
  • It executes npx lint-staged.
  • Lint-Staged looks at the staged file (file.js).
  • It runs the configured tools (e.g., prettier --write and eslint).
  • If everything passes: The formatted file is added to the commit, and the commit succeeds.
  • If a linter fails (e.g., ESLint finds an error): The commit is aborted, and the error output is displayed in your terminal, forcing you to fix the issue before committing again.

By setting up Husky and Lint-Staged, you automate quality control directly within the developer workflow, leading to cleaner codebases and more efficient teams. Happy coding!

entry.title: How to setup Eslint, Prettier and CodeQL
entry.summary: In modern web development, maintaining a clean, secure, and consistent codebase is paramount, especially when working on teams. This is where tools like ESLint, Prettier, and CodeQL come in.
entry.content:
In modern web development, maintaining a clean, secure, and consistent codebase is paramount, especially when working on teams. This is where tools like ESLint, Prettier, and CodeQL come in.

  • ESLint is a powerful static code analysis tool that finds and fixes problems in your JavaScript or TypeScript code. It ensures that your code adheres to specific stylistic guidelines and catches potential runtime errors before the code is even executed.
  • Prettier is an opinionated code formatter. Its sole job is to take your code and re-format it to ensure visual consistency across the entire project. It ends debates over spaces versus tabs, trailing commas, and line length.
  • CodeQL is a semantic code analysis engine developed by GitHub. It allows you to query your code as if it were a database to find security vulnerabilities and bugs. It is highly popular because it integrates seamlessly into the GitHub ecosystem.

Installing packages​

To get started, we need to install the necessary packages for ESLint and Prettier. We don't need to install CodeQL locally as it is provided as a free service via GitHub Actions and runs directly in the CI/CD pipeline.

Run the following command in your terminal to install the necessary development dependencies:

npm install -D eslint prettier eslint-config-prettier eslint-plugin-prettier eslint-plugin-react eslint-plugin-react-hooks @typescript-eslint/parser @typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin

Next, you will need to create the configuration files for these tools in the root directory of your project.

ESLint Configuration (.eslintrc.js)​

Create a .eslintrc.js file and add the following configuration to integrate ESLint with React, TypeScript, and Prettier:

module.exports = {
  env: {
    browser: true,
    es2021: true,
    node: true,
  },
  extends: [
    'eslint:recommended',
    'plugin:@typescript-eslint/recommended',
    'plugin:react/recommended',
    'plugin:react-hooks/recommended',
    'plugin:prettier/recommended',
  ],
  parser: '@typescript-eslint/parser',
  parserOptions: {
    ecmaFeatures: {
      jsx: true,
    },
    ecmaVersion: 12,
    sourceType: 'module',
  },
  plugins: ['react', '@typescript-eslint', 'prettier'],
  rules: {
    'prettier/prettier': 'warn',
    'react/react-in-jsx-scope': 'off',
    '@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars': ['warn', { argsIgnorePattern: '^_' }],
  },
  settings: {
    react: {
      version: 'detect',
    },
  },
};

Prettier Configuration (.prettierrc)​

Create a .prettierrc file to define your code formatting rules:

{
  "semi": true,
  "trailingComma": "all",
  "singleQuote": true,
  "printWidth": 100,
  "tabWidth": 2
}

Configure package.json​

To easily execute ESLint and Prettier, we need to add several scripts to our package.json file.

Update the "scripts" block in your package.json to include the following lines:

{
  "scripts": {
    "format": "prettier --write .",
    "format:check": "prettier --check .",
    "lint": "eslint \"src/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}\""
  }
}
  • "format": Runs Prettier across the entire project directory and overwrites the files with the properly formatted code.
  • "format:check": Runs Prettier in check mode, outputting any files that are not formatted correctly without modifying them. This is particularly useful for CI environments.
  • "lint": Runs ESLint targeting all JavaScript and TypeScript files within the src/ directory to catch errors and enforce code quality.

Ignore files​

We don't want our linting and formatting tools to scan compiled output, third-party libraries, or cache folders. To prevent this, we must create two ignore files: .eslintignore and .prettierignore.

Create both .eslintignore and .prettierignore in the root of your project and add the following folders to them:

node_modules
build
dist
.docusaurus
coverage
  • node_modules: Contains third-party dependencies which we should not lint or format.
  • build & dist: Compiled production outputs.
  • .docusaurus: Docusaurus cache and auto-generated build files.
  • coverage: Test coverage reporting output directory.

Testing​

Now the most important part: ensuring our setup works locally.

To test that Prettier is correctly formatting files, run the following command in your terminal:

npm run format

Expected Output: Prettier will scan through your project and automatically reformat any file that does not meet the standards defined in .prettierrc. The terminal will list the files it has processed.

To check for any potential code quality issues using ESLint, run:

npm run lint

Expected Output: ESLint will scan the files in the src/ directory. If your code is completely valid and follows all rules, the command will silently exit without any output. If there are code errors or stylistic violations, it will print a detailed report indicating the exact file, line number, and error/warning message.

GitHub Actions CI Integration​

To ensure no code regressions are introduced into the main branch, these tools are executed automatically in our CI pipeline.

In our .github/workflows/ci.yml file, we added steps to invoke both our formatting check (npm run format:check) and our linting script (npm run lint). If any of these scripts fail, the CI run will fail, blocking the pull request from being merged.

Additionally, a separate .github/workflows/codeql-analysis.yml workflow was introduced. This workflow initializes the CodeQL environment, builds the project (if necessary), and analyzes the codebase for common vulnerabilities, reporting them directly in the GitHub Security tab of the repository.

entry.content:
Welcome to my new blog! This space will be used to share my thoughts, experiences, and technical notes.

Docusaurus Blog Features Summary​

This blog is powered by Docusaurus, which provides several great features out-of-the-box:

  • MDX Support: Blog posts support Docusaurus Markdown features, such as MDX. This allows the use of React components (like interactive buttons) and Admonitions (callouts/tips) directly inside the markdown files.
  • Truncation: The {/* truncate */} comment can be used to limit the blog post size in the list view, keeping the main blog page clean and readable.
  • File Organization: Posts can be standalone markdown files or placed within their own folders, which is convenient for co-locating images specific to a post.
  • Metadata: The blog post date can be automatically extracted from filenames (e.g., 2026-09-17-welcome.mdx), and author/tag metadata is easily managed via authors.yml and tags.yml.
